subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
passage: Tushar had wanted this college since he was fourteen. Three years of coaching, 5 a.m. alarms, a wall of sticky notes. Now he was here, in a hostel room that smelled of new paint, and the monsoon had knocked out the power for the second night running. The corridor was loud with first-years laughing by torchlight. Tushar lay on his bare mattress. He should feel amazing. He'd imagined this moment a thousand times. Instead he felt oddly empty, as if someone had switched off the engine that had pulled him through every morning. His phone lit up: Ganga, his school friend. "How's the dream?" He typed great, deleted it, typed weird, sent it. "Weird how?" "Like I don't know what I'm for now."

qa.q: What knocked out the power for the second night running?
qa.a: The monsoon.

qa.q: Why does Tushar feel empty instead of amazing?
qa.a: The goal that pushed Tushar for years has been reached, so the direction it gave is gone, leaving a hollow, tired feeling.

qa.q: Tushar deleted "great" and sent "weird". Why was that honest choice useful?
qa.a: It opened a real conversation with Ganga, so Tushar isn't alone with the hollow feeling and can start working out a new direction.

qa.q: How might Ganga read "Like I don't know what I'm for now"?
qa.a: Ganga may be surprised, expecting joy, and might want to check in more often, gently.

grounding: A young man who reached his dream college feels oddly hollow on a stormy night in the hostel.

subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
passage: The acceptance email had come in April. Disha had screamed, Papa had handed out pedas to the whole building, and her photo had gone up on the coaching centre's board in Jaipur. Now it was September in Ahmedabad, and she was sitting on a bench outside the design school library at dusk, watching autos crawl past. Everything was fine. Classes were fine. Her roommate Mehak was nice. And yet Disha felt like a balloon two days after the party, still floating, a bit wrinkled. For four years every day had pointed at one door. She had walked through it, and on this side there was no next door painted on the wall. Mehak sat down beside her with two cups of tea. "You've been out here an hour." "Have I?" Disha said.

qa.q: Where did Disha's photo go up?
qa.a: On the coaching centre's board in Jaipur.

qa.q: What does "a balloon two days after the party" suggest about Disha's mood?
qa.a: It suggests a tired, deflated feeling; Disha isn't exactly sad, just drifting without the goal that used to give each day its point.

qa.q: What small step could Disha take now that the old goal is reached?
qa.a: Disha could talk honestly with Mehak and start exploring a new aim at the school, like a project or club, to rebuild some direction.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Disha sitting outside for an hour?
qa.a: Mehak may be gently worried, noticing Disha is off, and cares enough to bring tea and sit beside her.

grounding: A young woman at her dream design school feels deflated and directionless once the long-chased goal is reached.

subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
passage:
"So? How's the great hostel life?" Sumit Dada asked, dropping onto Mridul's bed.
"Fine."
"Just fine? You wanted this since Class 8. You made us all sit in silence during your exams."
"I know."
"So what's wrong?"
"Nothing's wrong." Mridul picked at the bedsheet. "It's just… I got in. And then what? Every day for four years had a point. Now I wake up and nobody's chasing me, not even me."
Sumit Dada was quiet. "When I cleared my bank exam, I felt the same for a whole year. Like I'd climbed a hill and there was just sky."
"What did you do?"
"Found a smaller hill. Then another. It took time."
Mridul almost smiled. "Help me find one?"

qa.q: Since which class had Mridul wanted this?
qa.a: Since Class 8.

qa.q: What does Mridul mean by "nobody's chasing me, not even me"?
qa.a: Mridul feels hollow now that the goal that drove every day is gone, with no new aim to push toward.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the talk, and what could the brothers do next?
qa.a: Sumit Dada sharing a similar year after the bank exam was the turning point; next they could pick a small new goal together for the coming term.

qa.q: What might Sumit Dada feel on hearing "Help me find one?"
qa.a: Sumit Dada would likely feel trusted and glad that sharing an old struggle helped Mridul open up.

grounding: A student home from a long-sought college admits feeling pointless, and an older brother shares a similar experience.

subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
passage:
I'm Zainab, and I got into my dream college in Delhi last July. I'd wanted it since Class 9; its name was on a sticky note above my desk for four years. When the result came, Ammi cried, Abbu gave sweets to the whole lane, and I felt like I was flying.
By October, I felt like I'd landed in an empty field. Classes were fine. Aditi, my roommate, was lovely. The campus was everything I'd pictured. And yet I'd wake up and lie there thinking, now what? For four years every morning had a reason: one more chapter, one more mock test. Now the reason was gone and nothing had replaced it. I wasn't sad, just quietly tired in a strange way.
One night Aditi asked why I kept staring at the ceiling. I said, "I think I miss wanting something." Saying it out loud helped a little. I'm still looking for the next thing to want.

qa.q: How long was the college's name on a sticky note above Zainab's desk?
qa.a: For four years.

qa.q: What does Zainab mean by "I think I miss wanting something"?
qa.a: Zainab felt empty and quietly tired once the long-chased goal was reached, because it had given every day a direction and nothing replaced it.

qa.q: What small step helped Zainab, and what could come next?
qa.a: Saying the feeling out loud to Aditi helped; next, Zainab could try new clubs or projects to find a fresh goal to want.

qa.q: How might Aditi see Zainab staring at the ceiling night after night?
qa.a: Aditi may have been puzzled and a little worried, since everything seemed to be going well on the surface.

grounding: A young adult who reached a long-chased college goal finds life oddly flat and directionless.

subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
passage:
Mentor's note, first-year engineering. Harish Nair, faculty mentor.
Ojas (18) came to our monthly check-in today. He chose this college as his first choice after years of preparation; his family held a small function when he got in. On paper he is fine: full attendance, average marks.
But he looked flat. When I asked what he enjoys here, he shrugged. "Sir, for three years I knew exactly what I was doing every day. Now I've got it, and nothing is pulling me." He said he sleeps till the last minute, not because he is tired, but because there's no reason to get up early.
He isn't in crisis, but I don't want to leave this. I've invited him to the robotics club's open evening on Friday and asked a second-year, Kunal, to walk him there. We'll meet again in two weeks, and I've told him the student counsellor's door is open if the flatness grows.

qa.q: Who will walk Ojas to the robotics club's open evening?
qa.a: A second-year student, Kunal.

qa.q: How does Ojas feel now that he has got into his first-choice college, and what shows it?
qa.a: He feels flat and empty, saying nothing is pulling him and sleeping till the last minute because there's no reason to get up early.

qa.q: How did Harish support Ojas, and why is it a wise plan?
qa.a: He offered a concrete new interest with a companion, set a follow-up, and pointed to the counsellor if the flatness grows.

qa.q: How might Ojas's family feel if they knew he felt hollow after the celebration?
qa.a: They might be surprised and a little worried, having expected him to be happiest now.

grounding: A mentor notes a young adult who feels hollow and directionless after reaching his dream college.
